content.overview: BNS s. 49 — Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment. BNS restatement of IPC 109. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 109. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 49 is the rule on “Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment”. The section provides that whoever abets any offence shall, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 49 exists so that “Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
49. Whoever abets any offence shall, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence

Essential ingredients
1. Whoever abets any offence shall, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A instigates B to give false evidence. B, in consequence of the instigation, commits that offence. A is guilty of abetting that offence, and is liable to the same punishment as B

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 49 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (b). A and B conspire to poison Z. A, in pursuance of the conspiracy, procures the poison and delivers it to B in order that he may administer it to Z. B, in pursuance of the conspiracy, administers the poison to Z in A’s absence and thereby causes Z’s death. Here B is guilty of murder. A is guilty of abetting that offence by conspiracy, and is liable to the punishment for murder

Exam use: quote illustration (b), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 49 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Explanations
Explanation.—An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment, when it is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment

learningObjectives: Master the default punishment rule for abetment under BNS s. 49.
Analyze the requirement that the act abetted is committed 'in consequence of the abetment'.
Understand the parity of punishment: abettor receives the same punishment as the principal offender.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 49 provides that whoever abets any offence shall, if the act abetted is committed in consequence of the abetment, and no express provision is made by this Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment, be punished with the punishment provided for the offence. Explanation: An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment, when it is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid, which constitutes the abetment.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: In the absence of a distinct specific statutory penalty, the accessory who successfully causes an offence to be committed is treated with the same moral and legal culpability as the principal offender and receives identical punishment.
statutoryFramework: Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt, BNS s. 49 (corresponding to IPC s. 109).
Condition 1: The act abetted must be committed in consequence of the abetment.
Condition 2: No express provision exists elsewhere in the Sanhita for punishing such abetment.
Penalty: Punished with the punishment provided for the substantive offence.
Explanation: Clarifies the causal chain — committed in consequence of the instigation, conspiracy, or aid.
essentialIngredients: The accused abetted an offence through instigation, conspiracy, or aiding.
The act abetted was committed in consequence of that abetment.
There is no separate specific section providing punishment for that particular abetment.
The abettor is liable for the full penalty prescribed for the principal offence.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 49 is the workhorse of accessory punishment in criminal law. It establishes full parity between the mastermind and the physical perpetrator when the crime succeeds. If A instigates B to commit theft, and B commits theft in consequence, A is punished under s. 49 read with s. 303 (theft) with the identical sentence provided for theft. The Explanation emphasizes causal continuity: the act must be committed under the influence of the instigation or in pursuance of the conspiracy. If the instigation was completely abandoned, and the perpetrator committed the crime independently on an unrelated impulse, the causal link fails.
examples: Teaching example (Parity of punishment): A offers B a bribe to give false evidence in court. B gives false evidence in consequence of the bribe. As no express provision exists for such abetment, A is punishable under s. 49 with the full penalty for perjury.

Teaching example (Causal link): A instigates B to set fire to a barn. B decides against it. Two months later, B independently decides to burglarize the barn to steal tools. A's instigation is spent; B's burglary is not in consequence of A's abetment.
distinctions: Act committed in consequence (s. 49) vs Act not committed (ss. 55/56): Section 49 applies when the offence succeeds; Sections 55 and 56 apply when the offence is not committed.
No express provision vs Specific abetment sections: Section 49 is a residual default rule; specific provisions (e.g. abetment of suicide under s. 108) override s. 49.
problemApplication: Issue: What is the criminal liability and sentence of an accused who hired an assassin to murder a business partner, where the assassin shot and killed the partner?
Rule: Under BNS s. 49, an abettor of an offence that is committed in consequence is punished with the punishment provided for the offence.
Application: The murder was executed in direct pursuance of the contract (conspiracy/instigation). No express separate section exists for general murder abetment.
Conclusion: The hirer is liable under s. 49 read with s. 103 (murder) and faces death or life imprisonment.
